### Problem: Frog jump {#sec-od-p4-frog}

::: {.p-statement}
Stones lie at strictly increasing positions, with $\texttt{stones}[0] = 0$. A frog starts on the first stone. Its first jump must have length 1. If the last jump had length $k$, the next jump has length $k-1$, $k$, or $k+1$, must go forward, and must land on a stone. Can the frog reach the last stone? Here $2 \le n \le 2000$ and positions fit in a 32-bit integer.

Source: [LC 403 · Frog Jump](https://leetcode.com/problems/frog-jump/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"The frog is on stone $i$" is not a state. Arriving at position 8 with jump 3 can reach 12; arriving with jump 2 cannot. Both greedy habits fail on the first sample: the longest legal jump and the shortest legal jump both die at position 8 with $k = 2$. The missing fact is the last jump, so the state is the pair $(i, k)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $dp[i][k]$ = the frog can stand on stone $i$ having just jumped $k$. The start is $(0, 0)$, a virtual jump of 0, so the rule $\{k-1, k, k+1\}$ allows exactly the first jump 1.
- **Transition.** From a true state, try $s \in \{k-1, k, k+1\}$ with $s \ge 1$. If a stone sits at $\texttt{stones}[i] + s$, mark it with last jump $s$.
- **Answer.** Some $k$ makes $dp[n-1][k]$ true.
- **Bound.** A reachable jump onto stone $i$ satisfies $k \le i$, so the next jump is at most $i+1$. The table is $n \times (n+1)$, not indexed by the position values.
:::

::: {#fig-od-frog}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
route = [0, 1, 3, 5, 8, 12, 17]
jumps = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5]
assert sum(jumps) == 17
def draw(ax, p):
    V.array(ax, p, route, index=False, label="stone", colors={i: "green" for i in range(len(route))})
    V.array(ax, p, jumps, 0, -1.7, index=False, label="jump", colors={i: "indigo" for i in range(len(jumps))})
V.show(draw)
```

One route on $[0,1,3,5,6,8,12,17]$: jumps $1,2,2,3,4,5$. Stone 6 is reachable and every route through it dies. The second sample $[0,1,2,3,4,8,9,11]$ is false: from 4 the longest jump that the rules can have built is 3, and $4+3 < 8$.

:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why an index table is legal"}
Each jump lands on a later stone, so $m$ jumps reach at most stone $m$. The first jump is 1 and each later jump grows by at most 1, so the $m$-th jump has length at most $m$. On stone $i$ the last jump therefore satisfies $k \le i$, and the next jump is at most $i+1$. That is why a column index of $k$ only needs to run to $n$, and why a position near $2^{31}$ never becomes an array index.

The same bound makes the inner scan stop early. Stone $j$ is reached from stone $i < j$ only by the jump $k = \texttt{stones}[j] - \texttt{stones}[i]$. Walking $i$ downward, $k$ grows and $i+1$ shrinks, so the first $k > i+1$ means every stone further left is also too far. After that test, $1 \le k \le i+1$, and the three columns $k-1, k, k+1$ lie inside $0..n$.

A jump of length 0 is not a move. From $k = 1$ the candidates include 0; accepting it writes $k = 0$ onto the same stone and the search never ends. Positions are added in 64-bit arithmetic: $2^{31}-1$ plus a jump overflows a 32-bit `int`.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
`can(i, k)` asks whether the frog can finish from stone `i` after a jump of length `k`. Try the three forward lengths and stop at the first success. `can(0, 0)` is the start. The false sample explores every failing branch; each extra stone multiplies that tree.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("frog", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "true"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def frog_rec(stones):
    pos = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(stones)}

    def can(i, k):
        if i == len(stones) - 1:
            return True
        for s in (k - 1, k, k + 1):
            if s <= 0:
                continue
            j = pos.get(stones[i] + s)
            if j is not None and can(j, s):
                return True
        return False

    return can(0, 0)
```

##### C++

```cpp
bool frogRec(int i, long long k, const vector<long long>& st, const unordered_map<long long, int>& idx) {
    if (i == (int)st.size() - 1) return true;
    for (long long s = k - 1; s <= k + 1; ++s) {
        if (s <= 0) continue;
        auto it = idx.find(st[i] + s);
        if (it != idx.end() && frogRec(it->second, s, st, idx)) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
Cache `can(i, k)`. The bound $k \le i$ says a plain `n` by `n+1` array is enough; a failed state has to be stored too, or the false branches are recomputed. The body is the recursion.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("frog", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "false"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def frog_memo(stones):
    pos = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(stones)}
    n = len(stones)
    memo = [[-1] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n)]

    def can(i, k):
        if i == n - 1:
            return True
        if memo[i][k] < 0:
            memo[i][k] = 0
            for s in (k - 1, k, k + 1):
                if s <= 0:
                    continue
                j = pos.get(stones[i] + s)
                if j is not None and can(j, s):
                    memo[i][k] = 1
                    break
        return bool(memo[i][k])

    return can(0, 0)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int frogMemo(int i, int k, const vector<long long>& st, const unordered_map<long long, int>& idx,
             vector<vector<signed char>>& memo) {
    if (i == (int)st.size() - 1) return 1;
    signed char& m = memo[i][k];
    if (m >= 0) return m;
    m = 0;
    for (int s = k - 1; s <= k + 1 && !m; ++s) {
        if (s <= 0) continue;
        auto it = idx.find(st[i] + s);
        if (it != idx.end() && frogMemo(it->second, s, st, idx, memo)) m = 1;
    }
    return m;
}
```
:::

#### Push set

::: {.form-next}
Keep, for each stone, the set of jump lengths that reach it. Stones are processed from left to right, so a stone's set is complete before it pushes. A forward jump never writes back into the set being iterated. The last stone is reached when its set is non-empty. This stores only reachable pairs; the sample has ten of them.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("frog", "push")
    assert str(final) == "true"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def frog_push(stones):
    jumps = {p: set() for p in stones}
    jumps[0].add(0)
    for p in stones:
        for k in list(jumps[p]):
            for s in (k - 1, k, k + 1):
                if s > 0 and (p + s) in jumps:
                    jumps[p + s].add(s)
    return bool(jumps[stones[-1]])
```

##### C++

```cpp
bool frogPush(const vector<int>& stones) {
    unordered_map<long long, unordered_set<int>> jumps;
    for (int p : stones) jumps[p];
    jumps[0].insert(0);
    for (int p : stones) {
        for (int k : jumps[p]) {
            for (int s = k - 1; s <= k + 1; ++s) {
                if (s <= 0) continue;
                auto it = jumps.find((long long)p + s);
                if (it != jumps.end()) it->second.insert(s);
            }
        }
    }
    return !jumps[stones.back()].empty();
}
```
:::

#### Index table

::: {.form-next}
Pull instead of push. The only jump from stone `i` to stone `j` is their distance `k`. It is legal when `(i, k-1)`, `(i, k)`, or `(i, k+1)` is already true. Stop scanning left once `k > i+1`. No hash map: the stones are already sorted, and the bound keeps every column in range.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("frog", "table")
    assert str(final) == "true"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def frog_table(stones):
    n = len(stones)
    dp = [[False] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n)]
    dp[0][0] = True
    for j in range(1, n):
        for i in range(j - 1, -1, -1):
            k = stones[j] - stones[i]
            if k > i + 1:
                break
            if dp[i][k - 1] or dp[i][k] or dp[i][k + 1]:
                dp[j][k] = True
    return any(dp[-1])

assert frog_table([0, 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 12, 17]) is True
assert frog_table([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 11]) is False
assert frog_rec([0, 1]) is True and frog_table([0, 2]) is False
for stones in ([0, 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 12, 17], [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 11], [0, 1], [0, 2]):
    assert frog_rec(stones) == frog_memo(stones) == frog_push(stones) == frog_table(stones)
random.seed(2)
for _ in range(25):
    n = random.randint(2, 7)
    stones = [0]
    for _i in range(n - 1):
        stones.append(stones[-1] + random.randint(1, 4))
    assert frog_rec(stones) == frog_push(stones) == frog_table(stones)
```

##### C++

```cpp
bool frogTable(const vector<int>& stones) {
    int n = (int)stones.size();
    vector<vector<char>> dp(n, vector<char>(n + 1));
    dp[0][0] = 1;
    for (int j = 1; j < n; ++j) {
        for (int i = j - 1; i >= 0; --i) {
            long long k = (long long)stones[j] - stones[i];
            if (k > i + 1) break;
            if (dp[i][k - 1] || dp[i][k] || dp[i][k + 1]) dp[j][k] = 1;
        }
    }
    for (int k = 0; k <= n; ++k) if (dp[n - 1][k]) return true;
    return false;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Recursion** is exponential. **Memo**, the **push set**, and the **index table** are $O(n^2)$ states with three moves each. The table is usually the fastest of the three: array reads, no hashing. Memory is $n(n+1)$ bytes, about 4 MB at $n = 2000$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $[0, 1]$ is true. $[0, 2]$ is false: the first jump must be exactly 1.
- A gap $\texttt{stones}[i] - \texttt{stones}[i-1] > i$ is an immediate no, because no legal jump onto stone $i$ is longer than $i$.
- Add positions in 64 bits. The triangular stones $0,1,3,6,\ldots$ force $k$ up to the bound.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Allowing a jump of length 0. It lands on the same stone and the recursion never returns; the set version inserts 0 into the set it is iterating.
- Adding the jump to a 32-bit position. $2^{31}-1 + 1$ is undefined in C++.
- Walking an unordered map instead of the stone array. A stone can then push before every jump that reaches it is known.
:::

**Variants.** [CF 505C · Mr. Kitayuta, the Treasure Hunter](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/505/C){rating="1900"} is the same $(position, last jump)$ state, maximising gems, with the jump stored relative to the first jump $d$. [LC 1654 · Minimum Jumps to Reach Home](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-jumps-to-reach-home/){difficulty="Medium"} allows one backward jump and therefore a BFS: the state graph has cycles.
